channel.title: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
channel.description: Posts in the discussion thread "becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation" - A small rant about why I don't like the direction the site has gone in the last few years

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded: Funnily enough, a lot of the criticisms raised here were subsequently addressed/explored in the 4-6 series.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I haven't been active in the community much lately, but I'm still a reader. I agree with Kalinin that the core of this site is quality creative content. I can also tell you that— compared to when I started here? The SCP wiki (counting content and forums, not chat enviro or whatever) has gone from a site tolerant of terse and hostile feedback with a fixation on in-jokes to a site much more welcoming, more demanding of quality feedback, and producing more diverse articles and tales.

From the perspective of a relative outsider, I'm not seeing a trend of decline, here.

edit: Seriously, though, all of this "hostile to cross-testing" …. writing that well is hard work. Make your own universe. Leave things out of your own work and then hint at answers in other pieces, or hell, in a Wanderer's Library piece. YOU CAN DO THIS THING. This is my primary motivation when coming up with shit; do it on your own terms if you are afraid of using someone else's skip.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I guess my point is: the standards and the opinions of people change with site culture over time, and by the end of Series 3 and into Series 4 we might undergo another shift in opinion of what makes a good skip and good narrative, etc. Maybe it's something you won't be so disillusioned with, OP.

yeh dis.

When you're a part of a major creative endeavor, tastes change as understanding of what you're doing matures and as contemporaries come and go. Biases develop, become the norm, and are later rejected. What's a rule of thumb now may later be discovered to have been detrimental.

There's always an element of rejection of established style to art. Many artforms have risen as deliberate eschewing of the mainstream. The SCPF is no exception. For instance, the weirdness of late Series 2 and early Series 3 can be seen as a rejection of the grimdark period that preceded it.

And, like Deci said, we'll probably see the pendulum swing back the other way, now that the weirdness has been the established mainstream for something like a year. Or maybe there will be a new, differet creative direction. Who knows.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I suppose it isn't now, but members are becoming afraid to publish an article, especially an SCP.

According to who? You? Either detail the extensive outreach you've done to come to this conclusion, or quit acting as though you speak for the community in general.

But I would like it if we slackened up on the strictness on tales.

I can't speak for the community, but speaking personally as a member of staff and both Forum and Site Critique teams: No. Absolutely not. In fact, tales, in my opinion, are not held to a high enough standard, due to their lower readership. The core value of this site is quality. We're not here to preserve feelings.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
but members are becoming afraid to publish an article, especially an SCP.

I feel like this can actually be a good thing, if it gets people to use the forums and/or chat correctly. I'm still relatively terrified when I post things to the site.

If someone's scared of posting, they should figure out why they're scared, and take the steps to rectify that if they can. Usually that involves learning to write at the standards of the site (which are, admittedly, pretty high. Most contributors have college-level or above writing experience).

People need to be willing to learn here. Everyone grows at some point. I remember my first post; I didn't get any feedback whatsoever, it was a generic magic object object what crazied you to death, and part of the experiment log included the phrase "scream recorded issuing from bathroom".

If someone really has what it takes to create material consistently up to the site's quality standard, then they won't mind putting in the effort to hit that mark. This site should be a hobby—the moment it's not fun anymore, that's an indication that a writing break is needed. Work on something else, do some reading, go for a walk, whatever.

Also, in regards to the tales… we've got hundreds of those, varying in rating, and frankly it's always more admirable to work your way up to standard rather than hoping for standards to be lowered to accommodate those who haven't gotten there yet.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
OMG! I agree with Crayne on something! :-)
I don't see that there is a fear of publishing articles, I see that there are a LOT of people coming online who are writing things that, for lack of a better term, simply aren't ready for prime-time. I wrote several SCPs and a Tale and mainlisted a couple. I had my heart crushed when they were downvoted into oblivion. I mean, I put all this HARD WORK and EFFORT into writing these great ideas! How dare people downvote my great work? Then, I took a step back, looked at what I had written, read more high rated SCPs from II and III, did more critique work and tried again. This time it worked. I think people need to realize that if someone is telling them that there is a problem with what they have written, it's not an attack on them personally, it just means there is a problem with what is written. There's nothing to be afraid of when you publish, but I understand why people are afraid. Writing is a very personal process, you're putting your heart and soul into your words and when people downvote, it feels like they are commenting on you as a person. That being said, it just means we have to pick ourselves up and come back as better writers.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
The main complaint here that I see is no intertexutality and not enough horror. In response to the first point, allow me to present a rebuttal or five. Intertextuality exists, you just have to put effort into looking for it in tales.

If I write something just as good as a famous early SCP, why does it deserve to get downvoted into oblivion and deleted while the early one stays popular, just because I was a few years late?

Because a lot of the top-rated SCPs (particularly the ones on the Heritage List) ain't that great. 087,093 and 701 are really the only "good" ones on there, in my opinion; the rest are up there because of ratings bloat. If you tried to write 343 today, you would get downvoted to oblivion because it doesn't meet current standards. The only reason things like 076 and 343 get away with it is because they're old. We've established this several times.

Honestly, this just seems like you complaining about two things, the first being SCPs you don't like. And you're perfectly entitled to do that, I just don't see why you need to make a 1500 word rant about it. You're free to post about it in the comments section of the SCPs.

The second thing you seem to be complaining about is the fact that what used to be considered good writing, like 343, 076, 073 or 105 is no longer acceptable. That's because we've moved on, and if your writing can't move on with it, well, I'm afraid we can't help you.

item.title: Re: Hey I can play this game too

item.title: Hey I can play this game too
item.content:encoded:
Maybe so, but they certainly aren't vocal about it.

Have you actually listened to people? Like, in chat, where you can read their opinions in real time, as of the current day? Cause it can get pretty vocal. I am not a quiet man.

As a newbie, I tried reading some tales, but they didn't make sense etc etc

We have these wonderful things called canons, which are self-contained series, with their own hub. We've got other series too. We have chat, where you can find all the background information you could ever need.

Yeah, the ones that are in series often take hours to read, and that's kind of a problem for a site that focuses on short stories.

Look, the longest tales we have on the site are a pair of novel-length works. Most of the others are pretty short. Novella length at longest, but those series conveniently split up into multiple parts so you can come back to it later.

The main storyline of ETDP is roughly 33k words, but it's split up into 15 parts. That's an average of 2000 words and change per tale. That ain't bad at all, and it's one of the longer series (Cool War is longer).

this site makes about as much sense as 4chan.

4chan makes plenty of sense. All it requires is that you have functioning observational skills. Same applies for this site.

You want to understand stuff? You put the work in.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
+many things were said
-close

Alright, here goes. First off, I'd like to say this to both you and Kalinin, and this post is kind of meant for both of you. I wrote that comment in a bit of a rush due to prior obligations, didn't say all I wanted to say, and came off a little rude. Sorry about that, but now I'll make my points clear.

A majority of the userbase despises most of those older articles that no longer measure up to our standards.

Maybe so, but they certainly aren't vocal about it. I tend to dwell in the comments section rather than the actual articles on SCPs and tales, and it seems that people on the oldie goldies just spam about how great it is, and that's often including the older members, not just the newbies.

I do agree that disliking an article solely because it uses a concept that's already been done before is kinda dumb, but if it doesn't execute that concept in a unique or interesting way to distinguish it from the all the other articles that use it, it's justified.

Then clearly you're different from the rest of the crowd. Without using an article from 2010, I give you the example of SCP-2189, an article that is, in my opinion, very well written, especially considering it's a second try. However, it's currently at +8, one reason of which, as stated in the comments, is that it's "basically 217." But, it's not. It's a completely different idea with only one mechanic remaining the same. Clearly, this site holds a lot of bias against things that have already been done.

The cat thing with 334 is dumb, though.

Yeah, it was. Cut me some slack, I was rushed and didn't have time to check the date on it.

Yes, they [tales] seem convoluted and unapproachable at first, but if you actually take the time to read a few, they won't.

Maybe some of them, but even so, that's precisely the point. As a newbie, I tried reading some tales, but they didn't make sense. I didn't understand what was going on at all, or who the characters were, or what the fuck a GOC was, but when I read the articles, I knew what was going on the whole time, and that's one of the things that makes the site so attractive to newbies. And added to that are the cross-testings, something that would get newbies to read other articles and find out what's going on there. So yeah, tales are fine, and some of them you can read without any prior knowledge, but a lot of them are only for people who've already read the articles. The articles are the core of the site, and that's why people stay around. Tales are supposed to just be supplements to add a little bit of narrative to the whole universe. But I'm getting off topic.

there is no tale on this entire site that takes "hours to read". Series, maybe, but not individual tales.

Your point being…? Yeah, the ones that are in series often take hours to read, and that's kind of a problem for a site that focuses on short stories. Now, that's not necessarily a bad thing, but once again, as a newbie, if you just read the tales, this site makes about as much sense as 4chan.

They're no more confusing or reliant on established canons as a majority of SCP articles are

Of course they are! The SCP format is literally designed to be read and understood in as short amount of time as necessary. When you're reading an article, you almost always know exactly what's going on, but when you're reading a tale, everything's different. Take when I read the Tales From The Bright Side for the first time. (I hate to use Bright as an example again, but this was actually the first time I read a tale.) I had absolutely no clue who any of the people or skips were. It plopped me right into the middle of this strange universe and expected me to have already read so many other things. And again, this isn't necessarily bad, it's just how the tales are different from the articles. But nobody reads tales first and has any clue what's going on. For another example, take the lolFoundation canon and the tale about King. How in fuck's name would a newbie understand the injoke of King and apples? You'd have to have hung around the site for a long time to be able to get that. And yes, I'll admit that there are some articles that do stuff like that, but,
1. Those articles are rare,
2. I think that they're a step in the wrong direction, and
3. They often are referencing other things on the site, and provide links directly to the source, and I'll say it again: this is one of the things that I loved about the site so much when I first joined.

If you continue to hold this view you're gonna be missing out on some of the highest quality works on the site.

Obviously, I didn't make this clear: I don't dislike tales. I like them a lot, in fact. But they are very confusing to someone who just joined that site, and crosslinking between articles is one of the major ways that newbies learn more about the site. If we rely on tales to bring us that, nobody's going to want to stay.

Anyway, I've talked too much already, and at this point I'm not even adressing anyone in particular, so I'll just finish off with this. I agree with Guilliman, and I think maybe we should all consider lowering and heightening our standards a little. I would hate to see more people start leaving the site than joining it.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
My opinion probably won't count as much as others, given how I've only started coming to the site two years ago and then took a two year hiatus but there are trends in what people like, and shifts in opinion as to what people think is best. This is especially evident when you look at a random Series 1 article (that hasn't been rewritten at least) versus a random Series 2 article and a random Series 3 article. Series 1 probably has the most variety of writing styles and concepts; the storytelling that emerged with Series 2, the sci-fi bent of Series 3, and the (relative) looseness of standards but prevalent horror-based theme that so much of Series 1 has. I mean, I can't say for sure since I wasn't around back then, but I'd imagine if you took a well-liked article from Series 3 that had so much emphasis on storytelling and worldbuilding and submitted it for Series 1 around three or four years back, people would flip their shit (in a good or bad way).

I guess my point is: the standards and the opinions of people change with site culture over time, and by the end of Series 3 and into Series 4 we might undergo another shift in opinion of what makes a good skip and good narrative, etc. Maybe it's something you won't be so disillusioned with, OP.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
Most people don't have attachments to old articles, though. In fact a majority of the userbase despises most of the older articles that no longer measure up to our standards. The only reason those articles are lingering around such high ratings is mostly due to rating inertia, where an article accrues tons of upvotes from ye olden days that take tons of downvotes to counter.
I do agree that disliking an article solely because it uses a concept that's already been done before is kinda dumb, but if it doesn't execute that concept in a unique or interesting way to distinguish it from the all the other articles that use it, it's justified. The cat thing with 334 is dumb, though.
My biggest point of contention is with your view regarding Tales. Yes, they seem convoluted and unapproachable at first, but if you actually take the time to read a few, they won't. They're no more confusing or reliant on established canons as a majority of SCP articles are, and there is no tale on this entire site that takes "hours to read". Series, maybe, but not individual tales. If you continue to hold this view you're gonna be missing out on some of the highest quality works on the site.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I've largely stayed out of this discussion, because people are free to like the things that they like, and a feeling of unhappiness at the move away from the simpler style of SCP articles is not uncommon these days. It's a legitimate reaction, even if I don't share it.

However, your summation of some the current practices on the wiki is inaccurate.

Nowadays, people jump all over you if you have an idea even similar to something already done.

This is not anywhere close to being a universal reaction among the membership. In fact, the most common feedback I've seen in the chat when a newer member asks if we have a certain kind of item on the mainlist already is that similarity isn't the problem, the strength of the narrative is. The recent success of multiple tooth-horror related articles within a week of each other in the recent past is a testament to this. I don't find this complaint to be based in the reality of what occurs among site membership.

And forget trying to do something that isn't completely alien and makes no sense at all. For instance, SCP-334, one of the most well-done articles I've seen to date, was downvoted solely on the basis that it was a cat.

Let me just clarify something before we go any further on this point. You're taking issue with the entire site culture nowadays because Bright downvoted an article in 2010. Really?

And this is by Bright, arguably the single most popular and experienced active member to date.

I wouldn't even call Bright "active" on the wiki these days. And again, your complaint is based on something that happened four years ago.

It's like people have an attatchment to the older articles, but if someone makes something similar, they automatically hate it.

That is not the dynamic. At all. Standards have changed, like it or not. People do not downvote because articles are similar to something to came before, they largely downvote because what's being written is not interesting in the current environment. Djoric wrote an article recently that was literally a rewrite of a Series I article and therfore the same exact thing, and it was largely successful. What people largely want now is story, a reason to care about something beyond "thing what does a thing", because "thing what does a thing" as a trope is pretty much exhausted. We've all seen it now literally a thousand times. People aren't downvoting articles of this nature out of some unthinking, knee-jerk reactionary outlook. They're downvoting because they objectively don't like it.

This is a perfectly fine discussion to have, but let's not base it on things that are either not really true or that make no real sense.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I said some of my thoughts in my response to Soulless, but I'll clear up my exact opinion here.

I almost totally agree with this. I'm also not that surprised that so many of the older members disagreed vehemently with what you had to say. This site used to be filled with great articles, both simple and complex. Nowadays, people jump all over you if you have an idea even similar to something already done. And forget trying to do something that isn't completely alien and makes no sense at all. For instance, SCP-334, one of the most well-done articles I've seen to date, was downvoted solely on the basis that it was a cat. Seriously. And this is by Bright, arguably the single most popular and experienced active member to date. Why can't it be a cat? Does everything have to be a platypus or echidna or obscure mollusk? It's as if the oldest members have this idea in their heads of everything having to be completely original or downvote. But somewhere along the line, "originial" and "flat-out bizzare" meant the same thing, which shouldn't be the case. It's like people have an attatchment to the older articles, but if someone makes something similar, they automatically hate it. Really, the only thing that I disagreed with you on was the -j. (Come on, man, that was adorable.)

item.title: Re: Breaking it down.
item.content:encoded: I agree with a good amount of what you said, Soulless, but Guilliman is absolutely correct about the crossovers. It is discouraged, and I for one am sad to see that. Remember the testing logs of 914 and 682? They were great, because they used other SCPs. Back in my earliest days, I always would read a new article and then envision what it would be like if cross-tested. Something about that just lets authors expand so much more on their idea. For instance, if you have a mind-control collar, it's a cool idea, but there's really nothing to it. But putting it on 682 or 173, now THAT'S interesting. It not only expands on the first SCP, it gives you a better idea of how the other SCP works. And yes, it's true that interconnectivity is very present in tales, but tales are often long, confusing, convoluted, in a series, or including references to shit you've never heard of. Articles, on the other hand, are easy to read, explain properly what's going on, never include any crazy shit written by some occult that seems to be translated directly from ancient Sumerian, and even the longest ones don't take hours to sit through. References in tales can be neat, but references in articles are entirely different. They make you consider all the possibilites and limits of something seemingly simple, and such things are DEFINETELY discouraged. I couldn't say why, but cross-testing is frowned upon and kind of seen as a thing of Series I, and that sucks, because that's one of the first things that kept me here. I don't know if the site's going to shit, but you can't deny that that is basically gone.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I'm in line with you on a lot of those points, Guilliman. A lot of the problems you have are inherent to how the site is set up. Instead of lots of intertextuality and useful SCPs, we have a metric fuckload of SCP articles that, due to their sheer number and different authors, would be essentially impossible to all connect meaningfully. Then again, this has been a problem since long before you or I joined.

I also agree with you that "wacky-just-to-be-wacky" SCPs suck, and that there are too many of them. Fuck them.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
Others have addressed the main points about this so I won't do some line by line. But I did want to note that I know where you're coming from on this, I've had similar feelings in the past, I actually mostly agree with your views on what's good. But it's not that the things you're talking about are "rules" in the idea of things being explicitly forbidden, but rather that it's a "rule of thumb", in that it's how the community will respond to certain things.

You almost never see cross-linking articles, useful items, or old-style articles succeed anymore these days. But that's about the COMMUNITY, not about the rules. If it were staff or some special delegation choosing what stays and what goes, then I'd agree with you actually. At that point the rules should be changed and those things be allowed because that'd be ridiculous. But since it's the community at large voting things out, then it's just a matter of being wistful for the old days and wishing these youngsters shared your values.

It's like seeing a movie that you loved get bad box office takings and get negative reviews(cough Serenity cough, cough Ender's Game cough). You can't be upset at the industry, just the general public for not liking what you like for whatever reason. But you're just one person in a crowd, and the crowd probably doesn't agree with you on most things.

If you leave, just keep in mind you're leaving because you don't find SCP articles as interesting as they used to be. We didn't drive you out or push you away, you yourself became bored with it. And that's fine. Interests change over time, and sometimes our interests change on us into things we no longer care for (cough Star Wars cough). It's life. If you stick around then cool. If you leave, then ok. Have fun wherever else you go.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
++ Hello! You had a lot to say!
Boy howdy.

"No helpful/useful SCPs."

… well, there is SCP-2722, which was published a couple days ago. Hardly not helpful. Not the only one, either.

There is also friggin' SCP-2000, and every Thaumiel article. True, their only raison d'etre is the use the Foundation makes of them, and so they are considered… uh, unpleasantly not exploitable, rather more like cheaty? Even hypocritical, I guess. But let's face it, this is the age of Thaumiel.

And, on old and new SCP items, you could call bullshit on the fact that many Series I items are garbage or have shamefully un-clinical tone. That's alright, many users do that already. So what?

Now, let's get to what you consider is becoming excessively frequent these days:

1. Being not all that interesting, but getting by through the use of a gimmick (different type of format, writing style etc.) This was cool the first few times they did it, but I really think it is getting overplayed. If you want a gimmick, at least have some substance to go with it.

How is writing style a gimmick? I mean, I can see why format screws, additional graphics and or media files or even weird CSS magic can be considered gimmicks, but from there to saying writing style can be a gimmick, pfeh, no. It's an artistic choice, same as the gimmicks, with the difference that writing style fits the story and the author to add to the story and improve on the author's writing capacity, whereas gimmicks can be simply add-ons.

Also, I regret to inform you that this is a multi-media site. We do things that transcend text. If the author wants to add gimmicks, they are free to do so, particularly when they believe the media fits a certain intention on their part. Sometimes, it'll be a hookie part of the article, increasing the interest of the reader on your stuff; that is, exactly the same as certain literary devices, but not relying on your capacity as a writer. Why should we constrain ourselves to text, when there is also sound, image, even video?

And, the "at least some substance" bit assumes that the gimmicks can't be interesting enough on their own. See, the SCP main list is a list (Captain Obvious, I know, bear with me) that allows us to compare a) with b), Series I with Series III, scary with weird; it also allows us to contrast SCP-087 with SCP-2557. Would you discard either from the main list? One is a long, scary story mostly based on text and a couple of images; the other one is reinforced by gimmicks but remains perfectly valid with a plain text, and still, the reason it racked so many upvotes was the absolutely inspired use of both, in consonance.

2. Being just plain weird. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it seems that since everyone is pushing the "only original ideas" thing so much, and most ideas are taken already, people start coming up with things that sound like they're out of a mad lib (seriously, the Mad Lib Joke SCP might actually have inspired some of these people). Being just plain wacky will only get you so far, at least in my opinion.

I know this is not the time to be self-pimpy, so I apologize. SCP-2073, the last thing I wrote, is more scary than weird, but it is both. It also relies on a gimmick to "reward" the reader. I assume the reason why you mentioned kaktus's excellent SCP-2740 is because you liked its oppressive, strange atmosphere and emotional push into fear and anguish; even then, Series I is not packed with things like that, I believe.

And, incidentally, most ideas are not even explored. Most tropes are, but tropes can be combined and served into original stories; going the spoopy way is a sure way to get you… well, not downvoted, not necessarily! Going the spoopy way is a challenge, like everything else. Thing is, we are more interested in motherfriggin' worldbuilding, and strange items, and wonderful anguish related to terrible misfortune instead of jumpscares, gore and "oh, well, we are all gonna die. Again." Most ideas on this front are still warm in our collective creative writing pool, and we choose to steer clear from them until that same collective pool goes to scares again, if we ever do it. Until then, we can all enjoy reading and writing cool stuff that is weird. If you, the reader, don't, don't worry! You can go back to series I if you want. :)

And lastly, yeah, Soulless got it right up above: This site runs on a democratic fashion. No one person can tip the combined motion of the entire audience. Do not worry, the month our skips are considered too over the top or stupidly weird, we will be giving a thought to scares, no doubt.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
I'm going to try and put this as succinct as possible. Not to change your mind, but to put certain things in context.

+ show block
– hide block

1. On "no helpful/useful SCPs" rule.

There is no such rule. Individual members may downvote any article that proposes or implies the use of a scip to the Foundation's advantage, but most members will downvote badly written scips that are used by the Foundation. All it means is that you need to bring it if you want to use it. So to speak.

2. On intertextuality

The discouragement of cross-referencing or cross-testing SCPs is mostly some kind of weird belief in the minds of members who parrot things they read on the site. How to Write an SCP explicitly talks about how cross-referencing or cross-testing is not discouraged in general, just really hard to do right. Just namedropping or cross-testing for the hell of it will get you downvotes. Doing it right will still get you downvotes because some members have this weird belief that it's a no-no, but it will also get you plenty of upvotes.

3. On double standards between old and new SCPs.

You're not understanding how this works. If you want old and new SCPs treated alike, everyone needs to continually think about all of their votes, and recast them as standards evolve. It's simply not feasible the way this site is set up. The only way to address this would be to have a committee of x people decide the fate of all articles judging each of them according to a strict set of standards, updated as time goes by. And even then, they'd have to continually keep going over the articles.

Of course, old articles still get upvotes even though they don't correspond to modern standards. That's due to a few reasons:

  1. Misplaced nostalgia (awww…look at the cute thing that does a thing, those were the days)
  2. Ignorance of current standards (new members start at 001 or 002 and upvoted pretty much every article on the way up the list.
  3. Divergent personal standards (some members just don't agree with current standards and like older articles better - their prerogative of course)

I'm sorry this site is losing its appeal for you. I hope you'll find your way back some day.

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
Wow, what a post. I'll see what I can do to respond to this. Keep in mind though, that while I'm a mod, I'm still relatively new to the site. I've only been here for the last two years.

This might be a little disorganized since I'm watching Frozen for the nth time with family atm.
hide

First of all, the "no helpful/useful SCPs" rule.

I think this is true in the sense that people tend to discourage weaponizing or excessively using SCPs, because it's too easy to go the wish-fulfillment OTT item route if the draft seems that way. Also, there's the inherent belief that the Foundation doesn't really know if they can trust items to work the way they do forever—after all, they're anomalous.

It comes down to whether there's a compelling reason for the SCP to be used. That said, there's also articles where anomalous items are made by the Foundation, specifically for use. For example, SCP-2332 was made to communicate between parallel universes. (I link my own articles because I feel confident that I've got the interpretation of those down for sure—I don't want to misrepresent other authors' narrative intentions when using them as examples.)

It just harms my suspension of disbelief, because I like everything to be interconnected in some way,

Yeah, after some people have approached me about it, I can agree. It is a little tough trying to encourage this though, given different authors have different wishes about their work. I'd like to see more people asking authors about crosslinking, myself, since I think it's fine to crosslink if the link makes sense in-universe and there's authorial permission granted so there's no misinterpretation of the work.

If I write something just as good as a famous early SCP, why does it deserve to get downvoted into oblivion and deleted while the early one stays popular, just because I was a few years late?

Actually, the Rewrite Team's been trying to work on that. People have been recruited to rewrite some of the older articles to bring them up to current standards, and we have an "article up for review" process that brings attention to some of the older stuff that either hasn't aged well or needs more people to look at it. It's been time-intensive, mainly because a lot of older authors aren't around anymore and getting the manpower (writerpower?) can be an issue. And of course, people do like the classics.

A lot of the old stuff is still there largely as relics of the beginning times, because they're relevant to the site's history. All the same, any Series I articles that fall below threshold are subjected to the same deletion process. The stuff that really doesn't age well either gets wiped off or rewritten. I'm not sure if there's much we can do about the high-rated not-so-great stuff, though. The Heritage Collection was created to address this, but I'm not sure what else can be done about the quality discrepancy. It does become an issue when people see Series I articles and assume it's still the norm.

There are still things written as an attempt to get to the classic SCP length and simplicity, though. SCP-2023 was partially written to achieve that sort of feel. Wonder of the anomalous, a sense of something more, but not an overwhelming amount of text.

If you don't know what I'm getting at here, let me give you a few examples.

The joke thing is understandably confusing, yeah. But when it comes to joke articles, if it's funny, that's all most people need for an upvote. The more people think it's funny or chuckle a bit at it, the more upvotes result.

As for the rest, if you're unsure about what makes them interesting, go to the discussion threads. You can leave a comment there if the responses posted by others aren't enough for you; there's nothing wrong with not liking something that a lot of people like. If people start to talk down to you because they feel you're excessively negative, tell a staff member and we'll sort it out.

Basically, I find myself not all that interested in the Foundation anymore, most new articles aren't to my taste, and I figure I just won't be visiting as often as I used to.

I'm sorry that this happened to you, then. I'm sure you're not alone in this.

I will say that I have had the idea to do a "return to classics" SCP contest sometime when I have the time, though. Maybe you would consider looking the site's way once in awhile, even if not as often? The contest will need judges, after all.

Again, sorry if this seems disjointed. Someone farted during the climax scene at the end of the movie with Anna and Elsa, and I'm still having trouble trying not to laugh. I've seen Frozen so many times but hey, context.

Hope this reply helps a bit or at least clarifies some things. Happy Thanksgiving~

item.title: Re: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
+ show block
– hide block

"No helpful skips" is really only enforced to avoid awful wish fulfillment skips, re: a giant laser sword that can kill 682 or a magical gun that can somehow negate 096. Like most cliches on the list, they're not necessarily bad in and of themselves, they're just incredibly difficult to pull off well, and that's why people tend to reject them. If you can make a good useful skip, then people won't complain.

Read Tales. Like, seriously. You want cross references? You want interconnectedness? You want a different take on existing SCPs? You want to see certain skips interact with other skips? Then go read some damn Tales. Honestly, do you even need a reason to read Tales in the first place? They play a pivotal role in the site and flat out ignoring them is just insulting to those who dedicate time to them.

Complaining about double standards in Series I and II/III is like complaining about how old school NES games are horrible by today's standards. I mean, of course they would, because today's standards weren't around back then and thus when they were released they were judged by old school standards. As Reject put it, most shitty old articles survive due to inertia; they get a substantial amount of upvotes from ye olden days to the point where they're safe from deletion and then it takes an entire legion of downvotes to drag it down. I'm sure if this site survives till Series IV or even V that people will look back on Series II and III and criticize it too. Standards change, and there's really nothing we can do about it. Just adapt and move on.

I agree wholeheartedly on the gimmick point. Style over substance, man.

I don't see why randomness is a bad thing. While I do agree that WTFery by itself shouldn't carry an article, I feel it does have a good place on the site; our articles cover a wide range of emotions, so why can't bewilderment and confusion be one? And I don't really see what you see in terms of the number of random articles being posted; the way you said it made it seem like every other skip being posted is an LOLrandom one, whereas I'd say it's like one out of ten or more.

Humor is subjective. You may have found the pun unfunny but tons of people didn't.

Since when did main list skips have to be entirely serious? 2662 is funny and goofy, yes, but it's not a -J. A -J is a skip where its entire existence in the Foundationverse is the joke, re: Santa, the Kool-Aid Man, the Kirby Vacuum Cleaner, etc. And I'm not exactly sure how it tried to be creepy at the end. Could you quote that particular segment? Because I didn't see it.

I'd say because it's digestible. Most of the higher rated skips have that rating because of their digestibility, i.e how easy they are to process and read. Short and sweet skips with a satisfying concept and a decent execution usually go over very well, even if there's not much actually there, because they're easy to pick up and read. I don't really like it, but eh, that's how the community likes things.

Good ol creep is great, and I did love that skip, but I don't think we should restrict ourselves to that genre of skip only. It stagnates creativity by not allowing skips that cover any other genre to be published and it's gotten to a point where with over 2400 skips written with a majority of them focusing in some way or another on creep that original and satiating creep is nearly impossible to pull off.

I agree with this. It's shiny and cool but at its core it's nothing special. I'm all for gimmicks with substance to them but putting a beautiful ribbon on a pair of socks doesn't make it more appealing.

Yeah it's weird, but I just find the idea of "ice cream hell" extremely interesting and thought provoking. I know what kind of weird articles you're talking about but this doesn't seem like one of those to me.

I really don't think that the reason Kalinin wrote this skip the way he did is due to the constraints of the format. If he wanted to write a Tale instead he would've. I think he wasn't ore exploring the constraints of the format rather than acting as a prisoner to them, testing the limits of how much story he could convey in a clinical scientific document. I see nothing wrong with this, and if anything it's a testament to how we're pushing the limits of what a conventional SCP is, not getting boxed in by a restrictive definition.

Good example of a gimmick with substance, yeah.

We definitely are as a site drifting away from our origins, focusing more on the entire spectrum of emotions and not just horror. Whether you like it or not is up to you. I really don't see how it's becoming more restrictive, though. Either way, if you're not coming back, then I hope you enjoyed your time here and goodbye.

And collapsed this too. - Crayne

item.title: becoming disillusioned with SCP Foundation
item.content:encoded:
Okay, first of all, no one here probably knows or cares who I am. That's not important. And doubtless there are people who will disagree with me, I know that. But my perspective on the site is just that it is pretty much turning into the opposite of what I find interesting, and what attracted me to it in the first place.

I'm speaking mainly of the general criteria these days for new SCPs. There are several universally accepted guidelines that I personally disagree with.

+ show block
– hide block

First of all, the "no helpful/useful SCPs" rule. Now I'm not suggesting the Foundation should have a bunch of superheroes, magic weapons, and alien technologies at their beck and call, but there should be at least some objects that can be used productively. I find it hard to believe that, in-universe, so few of these things could be beneficial, or useful. A lot of times it seems that adding drawbacks to them is done just to specifically avoid this. An example of what I'm talking about here is http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-896. Honestly, this one seems to be a typical "over the top item", it basically takes what happens in this typical type of game and applies it to real life. Only problem is you can't use it effectively because it screws you over, and even if you try to be smart about using it, it still screws you over anyway for no particular reason, just as a generic "fuck you". I don't find this kind of thing interesting at all. If it could be used effectively without such drawbacks, it would open up many other story possibilities.

That brings me to my next problem - intertextuality. Cross-referencing different SCPs and SCP concepts is completely discouraged. I know this is to stop people from trying to ride the coattails of more popular SCPs, or making things overexposed, but intertextuality has always been one of my favorite things in fiction. Reading a story about X which leaves some unanswered questions, then reading a (mostly) unrelated story in the same setting, which references X and gives you a new perspective on it, and makes you think "Wow, so that's what it was", or "I never thought of it that way before", or "so that's what happened to X". This is why I enjoy things like the interconnected cosmology of Stephen King's novels, or expansive shared universes like comic books.

I realize it can be hard to do this effectively with multiple authors, but having each SCP written as if it's completely isolated from the others always makes me think "Hey, why don't they try using SCP-X to contain this thing?" Or "Why not try what they did to SCP-Y to deal with this one as well?". It just harms my suspension of disbelief, because I like everything to be interconnected in some way, to get the real feeling that this is a shared universe, not just a bunch of separate stories linked by similar names and writing style. This is why I like stuff like Lord Blackwood's adventures encountering various other SCPs, or the test logs for different methods of destroying 682, even though lots of people hate that.

Another thing is the double standards between old and new SCPs. Many of the Series 1 SCPs, especially the first few hundred, would never make it past muster today, but they still retain high votes, and in many cases are among the top rated pages on the site. If I write something just as good as a famous early SCP, why does it deserve to get downvoted into oblivion and deleted while the early one stays popular, just because I was a few years late? I understand not wanting blatant copies or ripoffs of pre-existing stuff, but I'm talking about original concepts that just wouldn't be considered good nowadays but be lauded in the past.

Also, a lot of the new articles these days seem to fall into one of two categories:

1. Being not all that interesting, but getting by through the use of a gimmick (different type of format, writing style, etc.) This was cool the first few times they did it, but I really think it is getting overplayed. If you want a gimmick, at least have some substance to go with it.

2. Being just plain weird. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it seems that since everyone is pushing the "only original ideas" thing so much, and most ideas are taken already, people start coming up with things that sound like they're out of a mad lib (seriously, the Mad Lib Joke SCP might actually have inspired some of these people). Being just plain wacky will only get you so far, at least in my opinion.

If you don't know what I'm getting at here, let me give you a few examples. Using the "top rated pages this month" feature, I'll give my opinions on what is popular lately.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-649-2568-j

I really don't understand why this one is so highly rated. It's nothing but a feghoot - a long build-up for a corny pun at the end. Personally I don't find it funny, and I don't get how it is such a highly rated article.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2662

This one is better, but it's still basically a joke SCP in normal SCP's clothing. The idea of a reluctant Lovecraftian deity is amusing, but is this a serious SCP? It's funnier than the aforementioned J, yet they also try to make it serious and scary at the end, which, IMO, just doesn't work. Honestly it's basically a slightly more serious take on the "Sailor Cthulhu" Joke SCP (http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2006-j).

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2115

This is another "over the top" item, a dating site that connects to other planets and alternate times/dimensions/etc. instead of just Earth. Certainly some potential for story ideas or clever test logs, but I don't see why it's so popular.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2740

This is the first one of the group that I really like. It is incredibly creepy, atmospheric, all-around excellent. It might be similar to some stuff we already have, but it's just so good that I don't really care. This is the kind of SCP I come to the site to read about.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2505

I don't like this one at all. This is the kind of "gimmick" SCP I was complaining about. Take away the format gimmick, and all you have is 055, except it doesn't affect human memories. Even the gimmick itself doesn't make sense - any random person can choose what class it is, then type in something, and the letters magically become a description of 2505? How is that possible, if the information is not being stored outside of someone's memory somewhere? Is the implication supposed to be that the one reading the article is a researcher who has personally examined the thing, and is writing down what he/she learned? If so, what's the point, if the information will just be deleted anyway, before anyone else can read it? And why would it use the exact same wording each time, if it's a bunch of different people describing it from their memories? Also the tags give information about it, but the tags stay on the page without deleting themselves, further breaking the SoD. This one is a lot of flash and no real substance IMO.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2731

This is the other kind of SCP I complained about, the "wacky for the sake of wackiness" kind. Sure, it's weird. It's original. It makes you go WTF. But (and I stress, this is just my opinion), other than that, there's nothing really compelling about it. I don't find it to be particularly cool, creepy, or otherwise interesting. It's just weird to be weird.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2188

I might just be missing something here, but this one doesn't seem to make that much sense. I mean, it's well-written, it's interesting, it's probably my favorite of the ones I've covered so far next to 2740, but it just doesn't seem like an SCP to me, or it doesn't seem to read like one. It's more like a short story about people and their interactions. There's nothing wrong with that of course, but if that is the kind of thing that's getting popular lately with SCPs, it just tells me that the entire SCP format is becoming so restrictive that people have to write something completely different disguised as an SCP in order to have a good article. That doesn't seem like a good sign.

- http://www.scp-wiki.net/scp-2062

I like this one. It's an SCP-affecting SCP, which goes with that intertextuality thing I mentioned before, despite not making explicit references to other SCPs. It's also a bit of a gimmick/implied format screw, but it's suitably mysterious and interesting enough on its own.

Anyway, I guess what I'm trying to say is that the site has just been drifting in a direction that doesn't really seem promising to me, moving away from most of the things I liked about it originally and becoming something a bit too stodgy and restricted for my tastes. Basically, I find myself not all that interested in the Foundation anymore, most new articles aren't to my taste, and I figure I just won't be visiting as often as I used to.
